intro.html: Half of these words are about grabbing, and half are about letting go. Kings and crowns appear often, because power changing hands is where English needed the most exact words.

Taking: usurp (without the right), confiscate (by authority), appropriate (for your own use), commandeer (for urgent official use), wrest (by force or effort). Giving up: relinquish (let go), renounce (formally give up), repudiate (reject, disown), forfeit (lose as a penalty), abdicate (give up a throne or duty).
Ask two questions about each word: who has the right to the thing, and is it taken by force, by authority or by choice? The answers sort the words.

words.def: to take a position or power without the right to it
words.ex: The scheming duke tried to {usurp} the throne while the young queen was away.
words.ctx: The assistant coach began to {usurp} the head coach’s role, calling plays and giving speeches until no one knew who was really in charge.
words.etym: From Latin usurpare, “to take into use, to seize”: usus (use) + rapere (to seize).

mn.cue: you SLURP my soup, you SIT on my throne?
mn.text: While the king naps, the cat climbs onto his throne, puts on his crown and slurps his soup; it has no right to rule, but it {usurps} the throne.

scene.alt: A cat in a crown sits on the king’s throne beside his soup while the king points in fury.

words.def: to take something away by authority
words.ex: The teacher {confiscated} the phones and kept them in a drawer until the end of class.
words.ctx: At the border, officers {confiscated} the fruit from every traveler’s bag, since bringing it into the country could spread plant pests.

roots.means: to make, to act on (in verbs)

words.etym: From Latin confiscare, “to put into the treasury”: com- (together) + fiscus (basket, treasury).

mn.cue: CON-FISH-CATE: the CAT loses the FISH
mn.text: The fish seller catches the cat with a stolen fish and, as boss of the stall, takes it right back and locks it in the cooler; he {confiscates} it.

scene.alt: A fish seller holds up a fish he has taken back from a sad cat.

words.def: to take something for one’s own use, often without permission
words.ex: My little brother {appropriated} my best pillow and refused to give it back.
words.ctx: Rather than come up with her own idea, Tia {appropriated} her friend’s design for the poster contest and entered it under her own name.

roots.means: to make, to act on (in verbs)

words.etym: From Late Latin appropriare, “to make one’s own”: ad- (to) + proprius (one’s own).
words.note: As a verb it is said uh-PROH-pree-ayt. The adjective, uh-PROH-pree-it, means suitable: appropriate clothes.

mn.text: Pip plops down on Lila’s comfy beanbag, sticks a sign on it that says “PIP’S PROPERTY” and will not budge; he has {appropriated} it.

scene.alt: A boy sits smugly on his sister’s beanbag next to a sign claiming it as his property while she protests.

words.def: to take over something for official or urgent use
words.ex: The firefighters {commandeered} a neighbor’s garden hose to soak the burning shed.
words.ctx: When the bridge washed out, the sheriff {commandeered} every rowboat on the lake to ferry stranded families across the river.
words.etym: From Afrikaans kommandeer, from French commander (to command).

mn.cue: COMMAND HERE: this boat is needed!
mn.text: The flood captain points at the fisherman’s rowboat and calls out, “I need this boat for the rescue, right here, right now!” She {commandeers} it.

scene.alt: A rescue captain in a raincoat points at a fisherman’s rowboat and orders it into service.

words.def: to pull or take away by force or great effort
words.ex: Lila finally {wrested} the stuck lid off the pickle jar.
words.ctx: After years of losing, the underdogs {wrested} the championship from the team that had won it six seasons in a row.
words.etym: From Old English wraestan, “to twist.” Wrestle comes from the same word.

mn.text: Pip and the goat both grab the same rope; after a long tug and twist, Pip wrestles it free. He {wrests} it from the goat.

scene.alt: A boy and a goat play tug-of-war with a rope as the boy pulls hard to win it.

words.def: to give up or let go of something
words.ex: The toddler refused to {relinquish} the television remote.
words.ctx: After forty years running the bakery, Mr. Ortiz finally {relinquished} control to his daughter, though he still came in every morning to taste the bread.
words.etym: From Latin relinquere, “to leave behind”: re- (behind) + linquere (to leave).

mn.cue: re-LINQU: LEAVE it behind, hand it OVER
mn.text: After forty years at sea, the old captain hands the ship’s wheel to the new young captain and steps back; he {relinquishes} command.

labels.text: re-LINQU-ish: LEAVE it, hand it OVER

scene.alt: An old sea captain hands the ship’s wheel to a young captain.

words.def: to formally give up a claim, right or habit
words.ex: The prince {renounced} his right to the throne so he could become a painter.
words.ctx: After years of eating sweets at every meal, Grandpa {renounced} sugar entirely, announcing at dinner that he would never touch another cookie.
words.etym: From Latin renuntiare, “to report back, to give up”: re- (back) + nuntiare (to announce).

mn.cue: re-NOUNCE: ANNOUNCE you GIVE IT UP
mn.text: Standing on a chair at dinner, Grandpa Gus announces to the whole family, “I give up cookies forever!” He {renounces} sweets.

scene.alt: A grandfather stands on a stool and announces he is giving up cookies while his granddaughter gasps.

words.def: to refuse to accept or be connected with
words.ex: The scientist {repudiated} her earlier claim after new tests proved it wrong.
words.ctx: The club publicly {repudiated} the rude flyer that had been posted in its name, explaining that none of its members had written it.

roots.means: to make, to act on (in verbs)

words.etym: From Latin repudiare, “to reject, to cast off.”

mn.cue: re-PUDDLE-ate: toss it in the PUDDLE
mn.text: Someone hands Dev a rude note signed with his name; he crumples it and tosses it into a puddle, shouting, “Not mine!” He {repudiates} it.

scene.alt: A teen points at a crumpled note he has thrown into a puddle, angrily rejecting it.

words.def: to lose something as a penalty
words.ex: The team {forfeited} the game when only six players showed up.
words.ctx: Because she returned the library book a full year late, Maya {forfeited} her borrowing privileges for the rest of the summer.
words.etym: From Old French forfait, “a crime,” from forfaire (to do wrong): fors (outside) + faire (to do).

mn.text: Only three players show up for the big final, so the team must give up the game and the trophy without playing; they {forfeit}.

scene.alt: Three sad players stand beside a sign reading no game because too few of them came to play.

words.def: to give up a throne, an office or a responsibility
words.ex: The old king {abdicated} in favor of his daughter.
words.ctx: When the twins left the dishes for their mother night after night, she accused them of {abdicating} their share of the chores.

roots.means: to make, to act on (in verbs)

words.etym: From Latin abdicare, “to renounce, to resign”: ab- (away) + dicare (to declare).

mn.cue: AB-DIC: SAY it AWAY: “No longer king!”
mn.text: The tired old king lifts off his crown, sets it on his daughter’s head and says, “It is yours now.” He {abdicates}.

scene.alt: An old king hands his crown to his delighted daughter.

taking or giving up?
how
after.cap: Taking and giving up: who, how and by what right.

after.html: Appropriate has two pronunciations. The verb (uh-PROH-pree-ayt) means to take; the adjective (uh-PROH-pree-it) means suitable. “It is not appropriate to appropriate your sister’s pillow.”

items.q: In “The town will appropriate the empty lot for a garden,” the word is pronounced…
items.why: Here appropriate is a verb meaning to take for a use, so it ends with -ayt.

items.q: The team had too few players and had to give up the game as a penalty. The team…
items.why: To forfeit is to lose something as a penalty.

items.q: Which word means taking power without the right to it?
items.why: To usurp is to seize a position or power you have no right to. The others mean giving something up.
linquere means to leave: to relinquish is to leave something behind, to let go.
